question: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Mélanie Disdier (PfE), Antonín Staněk (PfE), Ondřej Knotek (PfE), Pascale Piera (PfE), Marie Dauchy (PfE), Pál Szekeres (PfE), Zsuzsanna Borvendég (ESN) Subject:

Created by the Commission in 1989, Jean Monnet Actions fund chairs, university courses and research on the European Union in more than a thousand universities. The Commission itself states that these programmes aim to support decision-makers and strengthen the dialogue around European policies. However, this funding raises questions about respect for academic neutrality. By exclusively supporting teaching on European integration, they can help to promote a vision that is essentially favourable to European policies, to the detriment of more critical approaches that emphasise the sovereignty of the Member States. 1.
Can the Commission clarify what safeguards are in place to ensure the academic rigour of programmes funded through Jean Monnet Actions?
Is the funding granted subject to an assessment to ensure that it is not used to promote a uniquely federalist vision of European integration?
Does the Commission intend to publish an independent assessment of the political and ideological impact of Jean Monnet Actions on European higher education?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE).
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.7.2026) The Jean Monnet Actions (JMA), part of Erasmus+, foster teaching, research and debate about the EU to deepen understanding while nurturing open dialogue, critical thinking and democratic engagement. Rooted in EU rights and values1, including academic freedom, the JMA support higher education institutions in academic teaching and research projects in the field of EU studies. The JMA support academic research, teaching and inquiry that critically examines EU policies and institutions. Projects cover diverse topics that reflect societal challenges, scientific priorities and policy-relevant research, and may explore critical or underrepresented viewpoints. Higher education institutions retain full autonomy throughout their projects. Several robust safeguards underpin academic rigour. The mandatory evaluations under Article 24 of the Erasmus+ Regulation2 provide independent assessments. The selection procedure is open and competitive, following excellence and merit principles to guarantee fairness and equal opportunities for all applicants. Impartial external experts assess the projects against predefined criteria published in the Programme Guide3. Funding decisions thus reflect expert evaluations and a rigorous selection procedure. Transparency and accountability are ensured through clear criteria, documented procedures, sound financial management and oversight mechanisms. The Commission safeguards procedural fairness and never interferes with the projects’ content. Beneficiaries remain fully responsible for delivering activities in line with their projects.
1 Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, OJ C, C 326, 26.10.2012,
